literal: (Datong year 1, that is, Wei Zhenguang year 3

literal: , and both state that Wei dispatched "Prince of Changshan Yuan Zhao" and others to command relief troops, and were defeated by Liang—that is, the "Yuan Zhao" of the epitaph.
idiomatic: —both say Wei sent Prince of Changshan Yuan Zhao and others to lead relief troops and that Liang defeated them; this is the Yuan Zhao of the epitaph.

literal: The epitaph does not record Zhao's relief of Woyang—probably concealed because of defeat.
idiomatic: The epitaph omits Zhao's relief of Woyang, likely because the campaign failed.

literal: This juan does not mention Liang's attack on Woyang at all, and Zhao's leading troops to relieve it is also missing.
idiomatic: This juan never mentions Liang's attack on Woyang, nor Zhao's march to relieve it.

literal: At that time there was only this one "Prince of Changshan"; "Shao" is a corruption from similar forms to "Zhao"—now emended according to the epitaph.
idiomatic: Only one Prince of Changshan existed then; "Shao" is a graphic corruption of "Zhao," emended here from the epitaph.

literal: The same corruption appears at juan 10 Annals of Emperor Zhuang, fourth month gengzi of the first year of Jianyi; juan 12 Annals of Emperor Jing, third month jiayin of the first year of Xinghe; and the Biography of Liu Siyi cited above—all are emended directly without separate collation notes.
idiomatic: The same error appears in juan 10 (Annals of Emperor Zhuang, gengzi of Jianyi year 1), juan 12 (Annals of Emperor Jing, jiayin of Xinghe year 1), and the Biography of Liu Siyi cited above—all corrected in the text without separate notes.

literal: Those who lease public fields pay one dou per mu: in all editions "dou" is written "sheng"; according to this book juan 101 Treatise on Food and Goods, Beishi juan 4, and Cefu juan 487
idiomatic: Lessees of public fields paid one dou per mu: all editions write "sheng" for "dou"; juan 101 here, Beishi juan 4, and Cefu juan 487
